title: Notes and intervals: the building blocks of music
description: You do not need to know every name before you start playing. Begin with the distance between two notes – and listen to what it does to the music.
keywords: Grunnleggende basics beginner Toner og intervaller: musikkens byggesteiner Du trenger ikke kunne alle navnene før du begynner å spille. Start med avstanden mellom to toner – og lytt til hva den gjør med musikken. Notes and intervals: the building blocks of music
content: One note is a starting point Play E. Then play another note. What you hear between them is an interval. It may feel narrow or wide, settled or tense. The experience depends on timbre, register and musical context. On guitar, one fret is a semitone. On piano, a semitone is the distance to the nearest key, whether white or black. E to F and B to C are semitones even though both keys are white. MODUS uses international note names: B is often called H in Norwegian notation, while B♭ corresponds to Norwegian B. Count letters and semitones Read the diagram as text Major third · 4 semitones: C4 → E4 Minor third · 3 semitones: C4 → E♭4 E–G–B on one string: string 6, fret 0: E2; string 6, fret 3: G2; string 6, fret 7: B2 From semitones to intervals Two semitones make a whole tone. C to D is two semitones. C to E is four semitones: a major third. C to E♭ is three semitones: a minor third. From C to Interval Semitones D Major second 2 E♭ Minor third 3 E Major third 4 G Perfect fifth 7 C, an octave higher Perfect octave 12 Counting semitones provides a useful map, but it is not always enough to find an interval's full name. We also need to look at the letter names. From C to F, we count four letter names: C–D–E–F. That makes a fourth. From C to G, we count five: C–D–E–F–G. That makes a fifth. Both notes are included in the count. Next, we use the number of semitones to determine the interval quality. C–F♯ spans six semitones and is an augmented fourth. C–G♭ also spans six semitones, but is a diminished fifth. On a standard piano using equal temperament, these intervals sound the same when played in the same register. However, they are written differently and can serve different roles in music. Remember two questions: How many letter names does the interval span, and how many semitones separate the notes? Listen before memorising First play the notes in succession. You hear the interval as a melodic movement. Then play them together to hear it as a harmony. Start with just two intervals, such as minor and major thirds. Compare them from the same root. The aim is to recognise a difference you can use, rather than collect as many names as possible at once. Describe what you play Choose one guitar string and play E–G–B. E to G spans three semitones, a minor third. G to B spans four semitones, a major third. E to B spans seven semitones, a perfect fifth. You are examining the same three notes from different starting points. Then play the notes on a piano or across several strings. The intervals depend on the pitches, not on the appearance of the shape. First explain which interval you expect, then check it on the instrument. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Play C–E and C–E♭ slowly, first in succession and then together. Sing the upper note before playing it. Repeat from D and E. title: Major and minor: one note makes the difference
description: A triad can change character when just one note moves a semitone. The third is a good place to start understanding chords.
keywords: Akkorder chords beginner Dur og moll: en tone gjør forskjellen En treklang kan endre karakter når bare én tone flyttes et halvt trinn. Tersen er et godt sted å begynne å forstå akkorder. Major and minor: one note makes the difference
content: Three notes around a root A standard major triad consists of a root, major third and perfect fifth. The formula is 1–3–5 . C major therefore contains C, E and G. A minor triad keeps the root and fifth but lowers the third by a semitone. The formula becomes 1–♭3–5 . C minor contains C, E♭ and G. C major C · E · G C minor C · E♭ · G Keep C and G. Move the third. Read the diagram as text C major · 1–3–5: C4 → E4 → G4 C minor · 1–♭3–5: C4 → E♭4 → G4 Major does not always mean happy Major and minor describe a chord’s interval structure. They do not assign a fixed emotion to the music. Tempo, rhythm, register, dynamics and surrounding chords all affect the expression. A slow major chord may feel vulnerable, and a rhythmic minor chord may feel energetic. Use your ear to explore the difference without forcing it into one mood. The same chord in different registers C–E–G, E–G–C and G–C–E contain the same three chord tones. When a chord tone other than the root is lowest, you have an inversion. On guitar, some notes may be doubled. An open C shape can contain several Cs or Es and still be a C major chord. A chord’s identity depends on the notes and context, not just the number of strings you play. Find the third in your own chord shape Play E minor and locate at least one G in the shape. G is the minor third above E. Raise it to G♯ while keeping E and B, and you have the notes of E major. On piano, hold E and B and alternate slowly between G and G♯. If G occurs in more than one place in the guitar shape, account for every occurrence when changing the chord. Raising only one of two Gs produces both a minor and a major third, not an ordinary E major triad. Read on: build the chords in a key ↗︎ FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Choose C major and C minor in the theory room. Keep C and G and move only E to E♭. Then listen to the same difference in E major and E minor. title: The circle of fifths: a map of related keys
description: The circle of fifths brings keys, key signatures and relative minors together in one map. Use it to understand chord connections, transpose your music and find a starting point.
keywords: Harmonikk harmony beginner Kvintsirkelen: et kart over toneartenes slektskap Kvintsirkelen samler tonearter, fortegn og relative molltonearter i ett kart. Bruk den til å forstå akkordforbindelser, flytte musikken til en ny toneart og finne et sted å begynne. The circle of fifths: a map of related keys
content: What does the circle of fifths show? Put C at the top. Go up a perfect fifth to G. Another fifth gives D, followed by A, E and B. Continue around the full circle and you return to the pitch class C. A perfect fifth is seven semitones, for example C–G. In the other direction you follow descending fifths, or ascending fourths: C–F–B♭–E♭. The octave you play in may change; we are mapping relationships between pitch classes. MODUS uses international note names: B corresponds to Norwegian H, while B♭ corresponds to Norwegian B. The illustration places major keys outside and relative minor keys inside. Neighbouring keys and a cadence Read the diagram as text Roots and functions in C major: F ← C → G; IV ← I → V; Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7; Roots: D → G → C G major · one new note: F♯: G3 → A3 → B3 → C4 → D4 → E4 → F♯4 Key signatures: one new accidental per step Starting from C major, which has no sharps or flats in its key signature, each clockwise step adds one sharp. G major has F♯. D major has F♯ and C♯. Going anticlockwise adds one flat: F major has B♭, and B♭ major has B♭ and E♭. Order of sharps F♯ · C♯ · G♯ · D♯ · A♯ · E♯ · B♯ Order of flats B♭ · E♭ · A♭ · D♭ · G♭ · C♭ · F♭ Neighbouring keys on the circle share six of seven scale notes. C major and G major, for example, differ only in F and F♯. They sit close on the map even though their tonics are a fifth apart. At the bottom you meet F♯ major and G♭ major. On a standard equal-tempered piano they use the same keys, but the notes are spelled differently: F♯ major has six sharps, G♭ major six flats. The circle shows common spellings; keys such as C♯ major with seven sharps also exist. Major and relative minor share a key signature The inner ring shows relative minor keys. C major and A minor have no sharps or flats. G major and E minor have one sharp. D major and B minor have two. The relative minor is a minor third below the major tonic, or on the sixth degree of the major scale. C major and A natural minor therefore share the same notes but have different tonics and different roles for their notes. Major Relative minor Key signature C major A minor None G major E minor F♯ D major B minor F♯, C♯ F major D minor B♭ B♭ major G minor B♭, E♭ In tonal minor, a raised seventh is often used as a leading note. E minor may therefore use D♯ in a B7 chord, even though its key signature only contains F♯. The circle shows key signatures, not every possible note in a piece. Find I, IV and V next to each other Choose a major key on the outer ring. Its anticlockwise neighbour shows the root of IV, the subdominant. Its clockwise neighbour shows the root of V, the dominant. Tonic I sits between them on this arc of the circle. C major F ← C → G Functions in C major IV ← I → V You can build C–F–G–C, or I–IV–V–I. Move the same idea to D major: D–G–A–D. The chord names change but the scale-degree relationships stay the same. This example uses major keys. In minor, you cannot simply read all chord types from the outer ring. In A minor, for example, Dm is common on iv, while E or E7 can act as dominant V or V7. Hear the fifths movement in ii–V–I In C major you can play Dm7–G7–Cmaj7. The chord roots follow D–G–C: two anticlockwise steps on the circle. These are descending fifths, or ascending fourths in a different register. Chords Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7 Degrees in C major ii7 → V7 → Imaj7 Notice that D appears as a major key on the outer ring, while the chord here is Dm7. The circle shows relationships between roots. Chord quality depends on the key and musical context. Also listen to B and F in G7. They can move to C and E in the tonic chord. The circle shows root movement; voice leading explains how the notes inside the chords connect the change. Read more about ii–V–I and dominant resolution ↗︎ Where do modes fit in? The circle of fifths is primarily a map of keys and key signatures. It does not tell you on its own which mode is the musical centre. C Ionian, D Dorian and E Phrygian all use C, D, E, F, G, A and B. They share the same notes but have different roots and interval relationships. D major on the outer circle is different from D Dorian. Use the circle to find relationships, and use harmony and your ear to decide where the music feels at home. You can keep one scale map through a progression while following which chord tones become important at each change. Read about modes and tonal centres ↗︎ A short practice routine First choose C major and play C–F–G–C. Say I–IV–V–I as you play. Then move the same pattern to G major: G–C–D–G. Next try D major: D–G–A–D. Finally, play Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 at a relaxed tempo. Sing the roots D–G–C and notice the direction. You need not memorise the entire circle at once; learn a few connections by hearing and using them. Use the circle without replacing your scale pattern G major and E natural minor share G, A, B, C, D, E and F♯. You can therefore use the same note collection over many diatonic chords from this family. The circle helps you find the key signature; it does not say that every chord should be major. Play Em–C–G–D and locate the chord tones within an area you already know. Notice that C major uses C–E–G, while D major uses D–F♯–A. You can keep the pattern even as the target notes change. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Open Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 in the chord workshop. Play and sing D–G–C and find the anticlockwise movement on the circle. title: From scales to your first improvisation
description: You do not need to use every note in the scale. A few notes, a clear rhythm and space between phrases are enough to get started.
keywords: Improvisasjon improvisation beginner Fra skala til din første improvisasjon Du trenger ikke bruke alle tonene i skalaen. Noen få toner, en tydelig rytme og rom mellom frasene er nok til å komme i gang. From scales to your first improvisation
content: Begin in a small area Choose E Aeolian, also called E natural minor, in backing tracks. The notes are E, F♯, G, A, B, C and D. Choose triads for Em–C–G–D, or seventh chords for Em7–Cmaj7–Gmaj7–D7. Start with E, G and B. These are the triad notes of E minor. Play one or two notes at a time and let the backing track answer in the gaps. You are practising making a phrase, not showing that you know a scale. A phrase also needs space Read the diagram as text E–G–B · three chord tones: E4 → G4 → B4 Call and response: Play: E–G–B; Wait and listen; Reply: B–G–E Give a small idea several lives Find a rhythm you like on one note. Repeat the rhythm and change only the last note. Then try the same notes with a different rhythm. This creates a clear connection between phrases. You can also answer a short phrase with a similar phrase. Listen for whether the answer feels like a continuation, a question or an ending. The pause between them is part of the music. A simple framework Play · wait · listen · answer A scale is a selection of notes All seven notes may belong to the key, but their meaning changes against the chords being played. A note that feels settled over Em7 may create more tension over another chord. Over time, explore the chord tones of each chord and land on one when the harmony changes. You do not need to move the whole scale map with every change: listen for new target notes within the same map. Change one thing and listen to the result Make a short phrase with E, G and B over Em. Repeat it with the same rhythm, but end on G instead of E. The third, G, can make the minor colour clear without requiring more notes. Then leave a pause before your response. Compare what changes when the pause is longer, the last note is sustained, or a note is repeated. Describe your choice in a simple sentence. The task has more than one musical solution. title: Modes: the centre matters more than the starting note
description: Starting a major scale on a new note shows how the modes are related. To hear a modal sound, that new note also needs to feel like the centre.
keywords: Modalitet modes intermediate Moduser: sentrum er viktigere enn starttonen Å begynne en durskala på en ny tone viser slektskapet mellom modusene. For å høre en modal klang trenger den nye tonen også å oppleves som sentrum. Modes: the centre matters more than the starting note
content: A centre gives notes their roles E Dorian uses E, F♯, G, A, B, C♯ and D, the same notes as D major. Yet the music can feel different when E is the root and the harmony supports E as the centre. If you simply play these notes from E to E over a clear D major cadence, your ear may still hear D as home. The first note of a scale exercise does not necessarily override the harmony. E is home. C♯ reveals Dorian. Read the diagram as text E Dorian · major sixth C♯: E3 → F♯3 → G3 → A3 → B3 → C♯4 → D4 Harmony supports the centre: Em7 → A7 → Em7; E–G–B–D | A–C♯–E–G; Let bass and phrase return to E Compare from the same root Parallel comparison makes colours easier to hear. Compare E Dorian with E Aeolian rather than moving the root at the same time as changing mode. Sound Formula Sixth degree above E E Dorian 1–2–♭3–4–5–6–♭7 C♯ E Aeolian 1–2–♭3–4–5–♭6–♭7 C Both have a minor character because they have a minor third. Dorian has a major sixth; Aeolian has a minor sixth. That one degree can affect both melody and chord choices. Play the same phrase over A Goal. Hear what the sixth does when the bass, melodic rhythm and ending stay the same. Before you start, review the minor and major sixth. Hold A in the bass for two bars in 4/4. In bar one, play E4–F4–G4–E4 as quarter notes. In bar two, play C4 as a quarter note and A3 as a dotted half note. Repeat with F♯4 on the same beat. Keep the tempo, attack and bass the same. On guitar, use the open A string for the bass. On the B string, frets 5, 6, 7 and 8 give you E4, F4, F♯4 and G4. C4 is at fret 1 on the same string, and A3 is at fret 2 on the G string. Exercise and answer Which note changes, and how does it sound against the bass? Transpose both versions to E and play them over an E pedal. Answer. F is the minor sixth above A and gives the phrase an Aeolian colour. F♯ is the major sixth and combines with the minor third C to give a Dorian colour. In E the phrase is B3–C4–D4–B3 | G3–E3, with C♯4 in the Dorian version. Listen for whether the bass and final note establish E as the clearest centre. Let harmony reveal the colour A vamp between Em7 and A7 can highlight E Dorian. A7 contains C♯, the major sixth above E. Let Em7 feel like home and use A7 as a contrast. You do not need to emphasise the characteristic note all the time. Try using it as a deliberate colour in an otherwise simple phrase. Modality concerns how music is organised, not how often you hit a particular degree. One fretboard pattern can contain several centres The notes of G major also occur in E Aeolian, A Dorian and B Phrygian. This is a relative relationship: the note collection stays the same, while the centre and interval relationships change. It does not mean a phrase automatically changes mode whenever it starts on a new note. Play the familiar notes over an E drone and then an A drone. Try ending on E and A respectively, and hear how the other notes take on new roles. A fretboard pattern describes positions; the music determines which centre is established. title: Diatonic modes: one note system, seven musical perspectives
description: Seven modes do not mean seven separate maps. Start with one collection of notes, learn to hear where the music feels at home, and use characteristic tones to create a distinctive sound.
keywords: Modalitet modes intermediate Kirketonearter: ett tonesystem, sju musikalske uttrykk Sju moduser betyr ikke sju separate kart. Begynn med én felles samling toner, lær å høre hvor musikken har hjem, og bruk karaktertonene til å skape en egen klang. Diatonic modes: one note system, seven musical perspectives
content: One collection of notes, seven possible homes A scale map tells us which notes are available. It does not by itself tell us which note feels like home . That depends on bass, harmony, melodic resting points, rhythmic emphasis and repetition. Take C major’s seven notes: C–D–E–F–G–A–B . Establish C as centre for C Ionian. With D as the actual tonal centre, the same material can sound like D Dorian; with E, like E Phrygian. No note has changed. The reference point against which we hear the notes has changed. Important: Playing C-major notes from D to D demonstrates the Dorian interval sequence. It does not automatically make the music Dorian. If the accompaniment establishes C as home, the ear may still hear C major even when the phrase begins on D. Same notes, different reference points Read the diagram as text C major notes · seven centres: C Ionian · D Dorian · E Phrygian; F Lydian · G Mixolydian; A Aeolian · B Locrian D Dorian · the sixth is B: D4 → E4 → F4 → G4 → A4 → B4 → C5 D Aeolian · the sixth is B♭: D4 → E4 → F4 → G4 → A4 → B♭4 → C5 The seven modes in one map Here is the family derived from C major. The final column describes characteristic degrees relative to major for major-type modes and natural minor for minor-type modes. Locrian is distinctive because of its diminished fifth. Mode Centre using C-major notes Interval formula Characteristic Ionian C 1–2–3–4–5–6–7 Major, major seventh Dorian D 1–2–♭3–4–5–6–♭7 Minor with major sixth (6) Phrygian E 1–♭2–♭3–4–5–♭6–♭7 Minor with minor second (♭2) Lydian F 1–2–3–♯4–5–6–7 Major with augmented fourth (♯4) Mixolydian G 1–2–3–4–5–6–♭7 Major with minor seventh (♭7) Aeolian A 1–2–♭3–4–5–♭6–♭7 Natural minor, minor sixth Locrian B 1–♭2–♭3–4–♭5–♭6–♭7 Diminished fifth (♭5), unstable tonic Ionian is the ordinary major scale and Aeolian is natural minor. Locrian is theoretically important but harder to establish as a stable centre because its tonic triad is diminished. Hearing modal differences is more useful than ranking modes by fixed mood words. Relative and parallel modes answer different questions Relative modes share the same notes but have different centres. C Ionian, D Dorian and E Phrygian are relative in our example: one connected view of the material. Parallel modes keep the same centre but change the intervals. D Dorian has D–E–F–G–A–B–C; D Aeolian has D–E–F–G–A–B♭–C. The difference is B versus B♭ : major versus minor sixth. Do not confuse these perspectives. Relative thinking helps locate notes on an instrument. Parallel thinking isolates what gives a mode its character . Both help, but they solve different problems. Same notes, new centre C Ionian → D Dorian Same centre, new interval colour D Dorian → D Aeolian Learn to hear the characteristic tone Take D Dorian. Play a quiet D bass or use Dm as the starting chord. Then play a short melody such as D–F–A–B–A–F–D . Notice B, the major sixth above D. Repeat exactly the same phrase, changing only B to B♭ . The collection now points towards D Aeolian. Keep rhythm and the remaining notes unchanged so you know you are investigating the sixth. Harmony can help: use Dm–G , with D clearly home, for Dorian; G major contains B. Compare Dm–Gm for Aeolian; Gm contains B♭. These are examples, not guarantees. If you play them as a functional cadence towards another centre, the perceived tonality may change. You do not need to hit the characteristic tone in every bar. First hear its effect, then use it as a musical choice . The fretboard: one connected map, not seven new boxes You do not need a new pattern at every chord. Start with one familiar diatonic map across the fretboard. It shows note locations; their meaning depends on the centre and surrounding harmony . The G-major collection G–A–B–C–D–E–F♯ can support G Ionian, A Dorian, B Phrygian, C Lydian, D Mixolydian, E Aeolian and F♯ Locrian. On the low E string, F♯ is at fret 2 and G at fret 3 . They are neighbours in one map. Moving from F♯ to G does not by itself change the music from Locrian to Ionian. Play a G drone under the phrase and hear G as home. Then place an A drone under the same notes and try to make A feel settled. Only an actual change of centre gives a meaningful modal change. The same applies on piano: bass and phrase endings do the work while the notes stay the same. Seven positions can help navigation. Connect them into one system rather than seven unrelated maps. Do not change mode automatically at every chord In a diatonic progression such as Em–C–G–D , G-major/E-natural-minor notes can work throughout. That does not necessarily mean four separate tonal worlds labelled E Aeolian → C Lydian → G Ionian → D Mixolydian. Chord–scale labels describe intervals above a chord root. Perceived modality concerns the music’s centre. A progression may retain an overall centre while its chords change. In improvisation, following chord tones, voice-leading tendencies and melodic targets can be more useful than changing the whole map. Ask at each change: Which note will I land on, and why? Keep the map and change the phrase. New scales become necessary when harmony or expressive intent actually calls for different notes. Write another ending using B♭, pointing towards D Aeolian. Changing one note changes the possibilities for harmony and melodic tension. Compare C Lydian with C Ionian: F♯ versus F. Compare E Phrygian with E Aeolian: F versus F♯. Keep the root and change one characteristic tone at a time. Modern rock, fusion and progressive metal can use this to choose melodic colours deliberately, even over a simple pedal bass. No mode guarantees one expression: phrasing, rhythm, timbre and harmony still matter. The method: hear, predict, play, explain, change Hear: Play the phrase with D as centre. Predict: Sing how the melody will change when B becomes B♭. Play: Check on guitar or piano. Explain: Describe how major and minor sixths produce different interval structures above D. Change: Use the difference for a new ending or chord colour. The aim is more than reproducing a scale: it is to hear, understand and use the difference in your music. Here “church modes” refers to the modern seven-mode diatonic system; historical church modality also used other rules, finals and authentic/plagal forms. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Keep D as centre and play D–F–A–B–A–F–D, singing B before playing. Change only B to B♭, listen and explain. Then play two bars of Dm–G and two of Dm–Gm. Which modal colour do you hear, and what creates it? Hear: Play a D drone and sing major and minor sixths without looking at the instrument. Predict and play: Repeat one phrase with B and B♭, keeping rhythm and register unchanged. Explain and change: Describe the interval difference and write a modal phrase with two parts. title: Roman numerals: the chords behind the numbers
description: Roman numerals describe relationships rather than fixed chord names. Learn the numbers first, then use them to understand chords in a key, transpose progressions and hear where the music is heading, wherever you play.
keywords: Harmonikk harmony beginner Romertall i musikk: forstå akkordene bak tallene Hva betyr I, IV, V og ii–V–I? Lær først å lese romertallene, og oppdag hvordan de beskriver akkordenes plass i tonearten – uansett hvor du spiller. Roman numerals: the chords behind the numbers
content: First: a short introduction to Roman numerals Roman numerals are an older number system also used in music theory. Before analysing any chords, learn three signs: I means 1, V means 5 and X means 10 . Combine them to write other numbers. Roman numeral Number How to remember it I 1 One unit II 2 Two units III 3 Three units IV 4 One before five: 5 − 1 V 5 Five VI 6 Five plus one VII 7 Five plus two VIII 8 Five plus three IX 9 One before ten: 10 − 1 X 10 Ten A smaller sign before a larger one is subtracted: IV = 4 and IX = 9 . After it, the smaller sign is added: VI = 6 . In ordinary functional harmony we mainly use I to VII, because we build chords on the seven scale degrees. Keep the degrees when transposing Read the diagram as text I–vi–IV–V: C major: C → Am → F → G; G major: G → Em → C → D; D major: D → Bm → G → A G is V in C, but I in G: G3 → B3 → D4 The chord name tells you what; the numeral tells you where Take C major: C–D–E–F–G–A–B . Build a triad on each degree by taking alternate notes. C–E–G gives C major, D–F–A gives D minor, and so on. A chord name such as G identifies the notes forming the chord. A Roman numeral such as V locates the chord’s root within the key being analysed . G is V in C major but I in G major. That is why the system is useful. Degree in C major Chord Roman numeral 1 · C C I 2 · D Dm ii 3 · E Em iii 4 · F F IV 5 · G G V 6 · A Am vi 7 · B Bdim (B–D–F) vii° Chord progression in C major C → F → G → C The same progression as numerals I → IV → V → I Uppercase and lowercase matter We use an important convention: uppercase numerals indicate major triads ( I, IV, V ), while lowercase numerals indicate minor triads ( ii, iii, vi ). A small circle, ° , means diminished: vii° . A plus sign, + , indicates an augmented triad, for example III+. Thus II and ii are different. Both have their root on degree two, but II is major and ii is minor. In C major, Dm is the diatonic ii . D major may appear as II , but contains F♯ and lies outside the key’s usual diatonic triads. We would often investigate whether it has a particular harmonic function. Remember: The numeral identifies the scale degree of the chord’s root . Letter case indicates chord quality . These are separate pieces of information. Move the progression; keep the relationship Take C–Am–F–G . In C major this is I–vi–IV–V . Now move it to G major, whose notes are G–A–B–C–D–E–F♯. The same degrees give G–Em–C–D . The chord names change, but the numerals remain. Key I vi IV V C major C Am F G G major G Em C D D major D Bm G A This is transposition in practice. Instead of memorising a song as disconnected chord names, understand the relationships. On guitar choose new shapes; on piano find the new chord tones. Roman numerals provide a shared language. What do i–iv–V and ii–V–I mean? Use the numerals to understand two common progressions. In C major, ii–V–I = Dm–G–C , or Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 with sevenths. The roots are on degrees two, five and one. The final chord is home in this key. The numerals describe chord relationships; they do not automatically determine an improvisation mode. In A minor, i–iv–V = Am–Dm–E . Notice that E is major . A natural minor contains G and would give Em as diatonic v . Raising G to G♯ gives E major a stronger dominant pull. That is why V is common in minor-key harmony. Analyse the actual chord and its musical context. Play C–F–G–C slowly and notice G’s pull towards C. Then play Dm–G–C. You reach the same home from a different starting point. Read on: ii–V–I and the pull towards home ↗ Sevenths, inversions and common misreadings Numerals can show more detail. V7 is a seventh chord on degree five, such as G7 in C major. The 7 describes the chord’s added seventh, not a move to scale degree seven. vii° is a diminished triad on degree seven; the circle is not a zero. In traditional figured-bass and Roman-numeral analysis, I6 usually means a first-inversion tonic triad, such as C/E. It does not automatically mean a C6 chord with added A. I6/4 means second inversion, C/G. Some modern pop and jazz charts use other systems; check the notation being used. Similarly, I–IV–V does not tell you to play Ionian, Lydian and Mixolydian in turn. It identifies chords relative to a key. Mode labels and Roman numerals answer different musical questions. Textbooks vary in notation, particularly for seventh chords and chromatic harmony. Here we use uppercase/lowercase for major/minor within ordinary functional analysis. Check the key first. Our method: hear → predict → play → explain → change Hear: Play I–IV–V–I in C major and listen for the return home. Predict: Name I, IV and V in G major before playing. Play: Check on guitar or piano. Explain: Why is D major V in G major? How can D major act as V/V when it leads to G in C major? Change: Transpose I–vi–IV–V into another key and write a short melody landing on a chord tone at each change. This takes you from knowing the signs to using harmony . Roman numerals are not music by themselves; they reveal patterns in what you hear and play. References: Open Music Theory – Roman Numerals and musictheory.net – Roman Numeral Analysis: Triads . Transpose it to G major without consulting the table. Check on guitar or piano and explain why Em is vi in G major. Read: Say I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII and translate them into 1–7. Build: Find C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am and Bdim on the instrument and label each correctly. Move: Play I–vi–IV–V in C and G major. Listen and explain what stays the same. title: ii–V–I: why chords want to go home
description: Three chords can create a clear direction. Roman numerals show their roles in the key, so the same idea can move somewhere new.
keywords: Harmonikk harmony intermediate ii–V–I: hvorfor akkorder vil hjem Tre akkorder kan skape en tydelig retning. Romertallene viser rollen deres i tonearten, slik at den samme ideen kan flyttes til et nytt sted. ii–V–I: why chords want to go home
content: Read the degrees within one key In C major, a common ii–V–I is Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 . D is the second scale degree, G the fifth and C the first. Here, lowercase Roman numerals indicate a minor chord; uppercase indicate major. The progression starts on a minor seventh chord, moves to a dominant seventh and lands on the tonic with a major seventh. ii–V–I names a chord progression, not a mode. C major Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7 Degrees ii7 → V7 → Imaj7 Follow the notes inside the cadence Read the diagram as text Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7: Roots: D → G → C; F → F → E; C → B → B G7 · B and F show direction: G3 → B3 → D4 → F4 Cmaj7 · one possible destination: C4 → E4 → G4 → B4 Listen to the notes inside the chords G7 contains G, B, D and F. B and F form a tritone. In a common resolution, B rises to C while F falls to E. These small movements contribute to the feeling of the dominant leading towards C. Other voice leadings and uses of the dominant are possible, but this is a clear starting point for listening. The voice-leading diagram shows that both chords contain B. The separate chord examples show B3 in G7 and B4 in Cmaj7, an octave higher. To hear B held in the same voice, play G3–B3–D4–F4 followed by C3–B3–E4–G4. Then play the transition again with C4 in place of B3 in the final chord. This gives you a C-major triad without the major seventh. Listen to the difference between holding B3 and resolving it up to C4. Move the idea without losing the connection In G major, the same kind of cadence becomes Am7–D7–Gmaj7. Chord names change while the ii–V–I relationship stays the same. Roman numerals make comparison and transposition easier. D Dorian can describe the notes over Dm7 in C major, but that does not make the whole cadence D Dorian. A collection of notes and a harmonic function describe different aspects of music. Follow chord tones within one note collection Over Dm7–G7–Cmaj7, you can start with the notes of C major. Then find F–B–E: F is the third of Dm7, B the third of G7, and E the third of Cmaj7. These are target notes, not a requirement to play a new scale over every chord. A simpler melodic line is F–F–E. F is held from Dm7 to G7, then moves down to E over Cmaj7. Compare the two ideas slowly and choose according to the sound, not the number of notes. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Play Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 slowly. Find F in G7 and let it move to E in Cmaj7. Then find B and try moving it to C. Sing the movements before you play them. Listen to cadences in the theory room ↗︎ CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING What do you remember? title: Triads: from the root to the chord’s three notes
description: Before adding a seventh, understand the triad. Build major, minor, diminished and augmented chords, locate the third and fifth, and play the same notes in different inversions.
keywords: Akkorder chords beginner Treklanger: fra grunntone til akkordens tre toner Før vi legger til septimen, må vi forstå treklangen. Lær å bygge dur, moll, forminsket og forstørret, finne tersen og kvinten og spille de samme tonene i ulike omvendinger. Triads: from the root to the chord’s three notes
content: What exactly is a triad? A triad is a chord class containing three different pitch classes that can be arranged as stacked thirds. In ordinary major/minor harmony, these are the root (1), third (3) and fifth (5) . A triad has three distinct chord tones even if the guitar plays six strings or the piano doubles notes in several octaves. Take C–E–G . C is the root, E the third and G the fifth. C to E is four semitones, a major third; E to G is three, a minor third. C to G is seven, a perfect fifth. Building triads by taking alternate scale notes helps find chords within a key. Remember that scale degrees determine the note letters selected, while intervals determine the resulting chord quality. The root stays. The bass changes. Read the diagram as text C · root position: C4 → E4 → G4 C/E · first inversion: E4 → G4 → C5 C/G · second inversion: G3 → C4 → E4 Four triad types: what changes? Keep C as root and change only the third or fifth. This makes each note’s contribution easier to hear. Type Formula Notes from C Stacked thirds Major 1–3–5 C–E–G Major + minor Minor 1–♭3–5 C–E♭–G Minor + major Diminished 1–♭3–♭5 C–E♭–G♭ Minor + minor Augmented 1–3–♯5 C–E–G♯ Major + major Major and minor have a perfect fifth and differ in the third. A diminished triad has a minor third and diminished fifth, six semitones above the root. An augmented triad has a major third and augmented fifth, eight semitones above the root. Write Cdim or C° for diminished and Caug or C+ for augmented. The formulas assume C is the root; ♭ and ♯ indicate changes relative to the major scale’s degrees. Find the triads in C major Use what you know from building chords in a key. Start with C–D–E–F–G–A–B and take alternate notes. This gives seven diatonic triads: three major, three minor and one diminished. Degree Notes Chord Numeral 1 C–E–G C I 2 D–F–A Dm ii 3 E–G–B Em iii 4 F–A–C F IV 5 G–B–D G V 6 A–C–E Am vi 7 B–D–F Bdim vii° Not every chord in the key of C major is a C-major chord. They share a key, but the intervals within each triad differ. Moving the system to G major keeps I–ii–iii–IV–V–vi–vii°, while the chord names change. Root position and inversions: same chord, new bass The notes of C major are C, E and G. C–E–G with C lowest is root position . With E lowest, arrange them as E–G–C : first inversion , commonly C/E . With G lowest, G–C–E is second inversion , commonly C/G . Root position C–E–G → C First inversion E–G–C → C/E Second inversion G–C–E → C/G The chord’s root remains C in all three. The root is not necessarily the lowest note. Inversions can make bass lines smoother and shorten voice movements without changing chord identity. In Roman-numeral analysis, I6 usually means first inversion and I6/4 second inversion. This does not automatically mean a C6 chord with added A. The 6/4 figures refer to intervals above the bass in figured-bass practice. Move one note and hear the change Spend time on this exercise. Play C–E–G slowly. Keep C and G while lowering E to E♭: C major → C minor . Keep C and E♭ and lower G to G♭ for Cdim . Return to C major and raise G to G♯ for Caug . On piano, hold two notes and move the third. On guitar, first play individual notes on one or more strings, then find a shape containing the same three pitch classes. The finger pattern is not the explanation; you are investigating the intervals . Describe what you actually hear. Major is not always happy, nor minor always sad. Timbre, register, tempo and context affect the result. Aim to recognise which note changed rather than memorising a fixed emotional description. From triads to seventh chords Once you understand triads, add one more chord tone by continuing the stack of thirds. Add B to C–E–G for Cmaj7 : C–E–G–B. B is a major seventh above C. Add B♭ instead for C7 : C–E–G–B♭, a dominant-seventh chord type. C7 need not be the actual dominant of the key; the name primarily describes its construction. Add B♭ to C–E♭–G for Cm7 : C–E♭–G–B♭. Root, third and fifth remain the foundation. That is why we learn triads first. Triad C–E–G Add a major seventh C–E–G–B → Cmaj7 Add a minor seventh C–E–G–B♭ → C7 Next: seventh chords, more colour on the same foundation ↗ The method: hear, predict, play, explain, change Hear: Play C major, C minor and Cdim as arpeggios. Predict: Sing the note that must move to turn C major into minor. Play: Check on the instrument and try all three inversions of C major. Explain: Identify root, third, fifth and bass in C/E. Change: Write a progression using an inversion to give the bass stepwise motion. For example: C → G/B → Am . The bass becomes C–B–A . G/B contains G–B–D with B in the bass. You have used an inversion to create musical movement, rather than merely learning a shape. Move from knowing which notes form a chord to understanding how those notes can approach the next chord. That makes maj7, m7 and dominant-seventh chords easier to learn. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Play C–E–G. Locate the third and lower E to E♭ without changing the other notes. Play C/E and C/G and name the bass of each. Add B to C–E–G and explain why the result is Cmaj7. Build C, Cm, Cdim and Caug from the same root. Sing the third and fifth before playing. Play C, C/E and C/G. Write the bass note and identify each inversion. Play C–G/B–Am and hear C–B–A in the bass. Then add B to the C-major triad and compare C with Cmaj7. title: Seventh chords: more colour, the same foundation
description: Adding a seventh to a triad brings a new shade of colour. Chord symbols become easier to read when you distinguish the quality of the third from that of the seventh.
keywords: Akkorder chords intermediate Septimakkorder: mer farge, samme grunnmur Når en septim legges til en treklang, får akkorden en ny nyanse. Betegnelsene blir enklere når du skiller mellom kvaliteten på tersen og på septimen. Seventh chords: more colour, the same foundation
content: Build on the triad A seventh chord has four different notes in its basic form: root, third, fifth and seventh. Notes can be doubled or moved to other octaves without changing the chord type. Chord Formula Notes Cmaj7 1–3–5–7 C–E–G–B C7 1–3–5–♭7 C–E–G–B♭ Cm7 1–♭3–5–♭7 C–E♭–G–B♭ Cm(maj7) 1–♭3–5–7 C–E♭–G–B Two independent choices: third and seventh Read the diagram as text Cmaj7 · major third and major seventh: C4 → E4 → G4 → B4 C7 · major third and minor seventh: C4 → E4 → G4 → B♭4 Cm7 · minor third and minor seventh: C4 → E♭4 → G4 → B♭4 Two questions clarify the symbol First ask: Is the third major or minor? Then ask: Is the seventh major or minor? Cmaj7 and C7 both have a major third but different sevenths. Cm7 and Cm(maj7) both have a minor third but different sevenths. In Cm(maj7), “maj7” means the seventh is major. It does not mean the triad is major. The brackets make this combination easier to read. Let one voice reveal the difference Keep C, E and G and alternate between B and B♭. You move between Cmaj7 and C7 with only one note. Then keep C, E♭ and G and do the same: now you are comparing Cm(maj7) and Cm7. The term dominant seventh describes a chord type with a major third and a minor seventh. Whether it actually functions as a dominant depends on the context. In blues and modal music it can have other roles too. See the triad inside the seventh chord Em7 consists of E–G–B–D. The first three notes form E minor; D is the minor seventh. Emaj7 consists of E–G♯–B–D♯. Here both the third and seventh are major. Keep the questions about the third and seventh separate when explaining the chord. First locate the triad on the instrument. Then add the seventh and listen to the difference. You do not need an entirely new pattern to understand the extra note. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Choose Cmaj7 and C7 in the chord workshop. See which key moves. title: Harmonic minor and Phrygian dominant
description: A raised seventh gives minor tonality a clear leading note. The same notes can take on a very different character with the fifth degree as their centre.
keywords: Modalitet modes advanced Harmonisk moll og frygisk dominant En hevet septim gir molltonaliteten en tydelig ledetone. Det samme tonematerialet kan få en helt annen karakter med femte trinn som sentrum. Harmonic minor and Phrygian dominant
content: The raised seventh in minor A natural minor contains A, B, C, D, E, F and G. Raise G to G♯ and you get A harmonic minor: A–B–C–D–E–F–G♯ . The formula is 1–2–♭3–4–5–♭6–7. G♯ is a semitone below A and can act as a leading note. It also lets the chord on the fifth degree have a major third: E–G♯–B, or E7 when D is added. One collection, two centres Read the diagram as text A harmonic minor · G♯ is the leading tone: A3 → B3 → C4 → D4 → E4 → F4 → G♯4 E Phrygian dominant · ♭2 and 3: E3 → F3 → G♯3 → A3 → B3 → C4 → D4 The same pitch classes: E7 → Am: dominant to tonic; E as sustained centre: modal use The fifth mode finds a new centre With E as the centre, the same notes give E Phrygian dominant: E–F–G♯–A–B–C–D . The formula becomes 1–♭2–3–4–5–♭6–♭7. The minor second F sits close to E, while G♯ provides a major third. This combination of ♭2 and 3 distinguishes the sound from ordinary Phrygian, which has a minor third. A harmonic minor A B C D E F G♯ E Phrygian dominant E F G♯ A B C D Distinguish function from modal colour E7 can act as the dominant of A minor. E Phrygian dominant can then offer a scale colour over the dominant before the music returns home to A. If E is instead sustained as the musical centre, you can explore the same notes modally. The harmonic experience is not automatically the same, even though the notes match. F to G♯ is an augmented second: three semitones. Use the leap deliberately and also try phrases that connect it through the root E or the fourth A. Limit the exploration to two differences Start with A natural minor versus A harmonic minor, changing only G to G♯. Then compare E Phrygian with E Phrygian dominant, changing G to G♯ while keeping E as the centre. In the latter comparison, the third changes from minor to major. Use one short phrase at a time and explain which note changes. This focused experiment shows the relationship without requiring you to learn every mode of harmonic minor at once. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Play E–F–E and then E–G♯–E over an E drone. Combine the two ideas. Compare with ordinary E Phrygian by replacing G♯ with G. title: Voice leading: the shortest path between chords
description: You can connect a progression by following the movement of each note. Some voices can stay in place while others move a short distance.
keywords: Harmonikk harmony advanced Stemmeføring: den korteste veien mellom akkorder Du kan få en akkordrekke til å henge sammen ved å følge bevegelsen til hver enkelt tone. Noen stemmer kan bli liggende, mens andre flytter seg et lite stykke. Voice leading: the shortest path between chords
content: Think of a chord as several melodies When you play four notes together, you can think of them as four voices. Each voice can continue to a new note in the next chord. A progression can therefore be heard as several small melodic lines. Voice leading is about this continuation. It is not just about which chord symbol comes next, but how the individual notes get there. Three common tones, one moving voice Read the diagram as text Cmaj7 · C–E–G–B: C4 → E4 → G4 → B4 Am7/C · C–E–G–A: C4 → E4 → G4 → A4 Follow each voice: C → C · E → E · G → G; B → A: down one whole tone Keep what already fits Cmaj7 contains C, E, G and B. Am7 contains A, C, E and G. Three notes are shared: C, E and G. One possible piano transition is C–E–G–B to C–E–G–A. The three lower voices stay while B moves down a whole tone to A. The final chord is Am7 with C in the bass, or first inversion. Cmaj7 C · E · G · B Am7/C C · E · G · A The nearest path is a choice Small movements can bring calm and continuity. Larger leaps, a change of register or a new bass note may be right when you want contrast and direction. Good voice leading does not mean every voice must always move as little as possible. On guitar, the construction of the shapes affects what is practical. A shape may double notes or omit a perfect fifth. Consider both the voices you actually play and the musical role you want to highlight. Try treating the highest voice as a clear melodic line. It can give your chord playing its own story even when the rest of the harmony is simple. Follow the voice you actually hear Play C–E–G–B followed by C–E–G–A, listening only to B–A at the top. Then play this line alone. Restore the other notes and see whether you can still hear the movement as a separate melody. On guitar, you can choose a smaller shape that makes this voice clear. The aim here is to see common tones and movement in a concrete example, rather than cover every rule of part-writing. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Build Cmaj7–Am7 in the chord workshop. title: Rhythm in 7/8: groups that feel natural
description: Seven eighth notes need not feel like a long count to seven. Small groups make it easier to find a groove and keep your direction.
keywords: Rytmikk rhythm advanced Rytme i 7/8: grupper som føles naturlige Sju åttendedeler trenger ikke oppleves som en lang telling til sju. Små grupper gjør det lettere å finne et groove og beholde retningen. Rhythm in 7/8: groups that feel natural
content: What does 7/8 tell you? A bar of 7/8 contains seven eighth notes. The upper number in the time signature tells you how many note values the bar contains; the lower number identifies the eighth-note value. This does not mean all seven pulses need equal emphasis. Grouping the eighth notes lets you feel a larger movement through the bar. The same seven eighths, a new emphasis Read the diagram as text 7/8 · 2 + 2 + 3: 2+2+3 eighths; accents on 1, 3, 5 7/8 · 3 + 2 + 2: 3+2+2 eighths; accents on 1, 4, 6 Try 2 + 2 + 3 A common grouping is two, two and three eighth notes. Count one-two | one-two | one-two-three , placing a stronger accent at the start of each group. 1 · 2 1 · 2 1 · 2 · 3 Another option is 3 + 2 + 2. There are still seven eighth notes, but the accent positions change the feel of the bar. You hear different groupings, not a new number of notes. Let a simple phrase land Begin on one note. Play or clap the start of each group and keep the inner eighth-note pulse steady. Once that feels comfortable, add short notes or rests between the accents. Gradually let your melody span several bars. A phrase need not end at every bar line. You can keep the accompaniment’s grouping while giving the melody a longer arc. The MODUS backing track tool currently uses 4/4. Practise this 7/8 example with your own counting or a metronome that supports grouping in seven. Keep the pulse when the accents move Count seven even eighth notes. In 2+2+3, the group starts are at positions 1, 3 and 5. In 3+2+2, they are at 1, 4 and 6. Clap only these positions while continuing to feel all seven eighth notes. Switch grouping after four bars while keeping the same tempo. If you speed up in the group of three, return to counting without the instrument before adding notes again. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Clap 2 + 2 + 3 for four bars without speeding up the final group. Then play E on the first eighth note of each group. Switch to 3 + 2 + 2 and notice the difference. title: Build the chords in a key
description: Building triads from scale notes gives you a family of chords. G major shows how notes, chord names and Roman numerals connect.
keywords: Akkorder chords beginner Bygg akkordene i en toneart Når du bygger treklanger av skalatonene, får du en familie av akkorder. G-dur viser hvordan tonene, akkordnavnene og romertallene henger sammen. Build the chords in a key
content: Start with the notes, not the shapes G major consists of G, A, B, C, D, E and F♯. Choose G as the root and take alternate scale notes: G–B–D. This produces a G major triad. Start on A and do the same: A–C–E. This time you get A minor. The distances between the notes determine the chord quality. G–B is a major third, while A–C is a minor third. That is why the chords are not all major, even though you are using a major scale. Stack alternate scale notes in G major Read the diagram as text The seven triads of G major: I: G–B–D · ii: A–C–E; iii: B–D–F♯ · IV: C–E–G; V: D–F♯–A · vi: E–G–B; vii°: F♯–A–C F♯dim · minor third, diminished fifth: F♯3 → A3 → C4 The seven triads in G major Continue from each scale degree using only notes from G major. After F♯, continue with G in the next octave. The chords are G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em and F♯dim. The notes are G–B–D, A–C–E, B–D–F♯, C–E–G, D–F♯–A, E–G–B and F♯–A–C. The final triad is diminished: above F♯ it has a minor third, A, and a diminished fifth, C. Roman numerals show the pattern In G major, the sequence is I–ii–iii–IV–V–vi–vii°. Uppercase numerals indicate major, lowercase indicate minor, and the small circle indicates a diminished triad. This pattern applies to diatonic triads in every major key. Try I–V–vi–IV: G–D–Em–C. Move the same degree pattern to C major and it becomes C–G–Am–F. The notes and shapes change, while the relationship between the degrees remains. The same notes can have a different home E natural minor uses the same notes as G major. Yet Em is the first degree when E is the centre, and the sixth degree in G major. Choose the reference key before assigning Roman numerals to a progression. Diatonic here means that the chord tones come from the selected scale. Music can also use chords outside this family. First learn to recognise the pattern; later departures will then be easier to understand. One step further: ii–V–I with sevenths Once you are comfortable with triads, add another note by continuing with alternate scale notes. In C major, D–F–A–C gives Dm7, G–B–D–F gives G7, and C–E–G–B gives Cmaj7. These are the second, fifth and first degrees: ii7–V7–Imaj7. This is an optional extension of the triad exercise. You still use only C, D, E, F, G, A and B. Listen for the arrival on Cmaj7; you do not need to master new shapes at full speed. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Write the notes of G, Am and D before playing them. Then play G–D–Em–C and say I–V–vi–IV. Move the same pattern to C major and check which notes change. Start with the triads in the exercise above. Write down and check the notes before playing. To try the seventh-chord sound, open Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 with the button below. Listen first, then play one chord per bar at 60 BPM. On guitar, choose a shape you can reach calmly; on piano, you can play the root first and then the remaining chord tones. Say ii7–V7–Imaj7 as you play. Notice which notes change and listen for the arrival on Cmaj7. Change the tonic to D and keep Ionian. Expect Em7–A7–Dmaj7. Check this before listening. title: One scale pattern, new target notes
description: You can keep one familiar scale pattern through a progression while still following the harmony. The key is to see which notes in the pattern belong to the current chord.
keywords: Improvisasjon improvisation intermediate Ett skalakart, nye måltoner Du kan beholde ett kjent skalakart gjennom en akkordrekke og likevel følge harmonien. Nøkkelen er å se hvilke toner i kartet som tilhører akkorden akkurat nå. One scale pattern, new target notes
content: A shared note collection Use Em–C–G–D as an example. All four triads can be built from E, F♯, G, A, B, C and D. This is the note collection of E natural minor and G major. Find the notes in a fretboard area you already know, or on piano. Keep that area throughout the progression. You do not need to switch to a new physical scale pattern for each chord. One note collection. New thirds. Read the diagram as text Em → C → G → D: Third: G → E → B → F♯; Roots: E → C → G → D All target notes belong to the collection: E3 → F♯3 → G3 → A3 → B3 → C4 → D4 The chord highlights different notes The chord tones are E–G–B in Em, C–E–G in C, G–B–D in G and D–F♯–A in D. They all lie within the same pattern. What changes is which notes serve as the root, third and fifth of the current chord. G is the minor third of Em, the perfect fifth of C and the root of G. Over D, G is a fourth above the root and is not part of the D major triad. The same note can therefore have a different effect when the chord changes. Choose one target note per chord Start with the roots E–C–G–D. Play one note at each chord change. Then try the thirds G–E–B–F♯. Both lines follow the harmony without requiring a new scale for each change. Once the target notes feel secure, add one or two scale notes on the way to them. Notes outside the chord can act as passing notes, colour or tension. Their duration, rhythm and subsequent movement affect how they sound. One pattern is a starting point, not a rule The method works here because the chords share a diatonic note collection. If the progression introduces a note outside the scale, listen to and examine the new relationship. One fixed pattern will not necessarily fit every part of every piece. The point is to connect a familiar pattern to the harmony. Later you can extend the range or explore other colours. Let that be a musical choice, rather than an automatic requirement to use four different patterns over four chords. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Play Em–C–G–D slowly. First use only E–C–G–D as targets, then G–E–B–F♯. Finally make a short phrase that lands on a chosen chord tone at each change. title: Dorian and Aeolian: same tonic, new colour
description: Keep E as home and compare C with C♯. Changing just one scale degree makes the difference between Aeolian and Dorian easier to explore with both your ear and your instrument.
keywords: Modalitet modes intermediate Dorisk og eolisk: samme grunntone, ny farge Behold E som hjem og sammenlign C med C♯. Når bare ett skalatrinn endres, blir forskjellen mellom eolisk og dorisk lettere å undersøke med både øret og instrumentet. Dorian and Aeolian: same tonic, new colour
content: Keep the tonic fixed E Aeolian, or E natural minor, has E–F♯–G–A–B–C–D. E Dorian has E–F♯–G–A–B–C♯–D. Six of the seven notes are shared. The difference is the minor sixth, C, versus the major sixth, C♯, measured from E. Both have a minor third, G, and a minor seventh, D. Dorian therefore retains a minor character even though its sixth is major. This comparison concerns the interval structure, not a fixed rule for how the music must feel. Keep E. Change only the sixth. Read the diagram as text E Aeolian · C is the minor sixth: E3 → F♯3 → G3 → A3 → B3 → C4 → D4 E Dorian · C♯ is the major sixth: E3 → F♯3 → G3 → A3 → B3 → C♯4 → D4 Same bass, two harmonic fields: Aeolian: Em → Am → Em; Dorian: Em → A → Em Change one note in a short phrase Play E–G–B–C–B–G–E slowly over an E drone. Then replace only C with C♯. Keep the rhythm, register and duration as similar as possible so you are examining the pitch change rather than several changes at once. Then try sustaining C or C♯ a little longer before moving to B. Notice that C is a half step above B, while C♯ is a whole step above B. Describe the difference you hear without searching for one mandatory emotion word. Let the chords support the comparison Em–Am can support E Aeolian when Em feels like home. Am contains A–C–E. Replace Am with A major and C becomes C♯: A–C♯–E. Em–A can therefore support E Dorian. With E as the reference, this is i–iv versus i–IV. The lowercase or uppercase numeral describes the chord quality. A progression alone does not guarantee how the centre is heard; use the bass, phrasing and return to Em to establish E clearly. Distinguish parallel and relative comparisons E Aeolian and E Dorian are compared in parallel: the same tonic, with one changed scale degree. G major and E Aeolian are relative: the same notes, with different centres. The two comparisons answer different questions. Finally move the experiment to A. A Aeolian has F, while A Dorian has F♯. Keep the other notes A, B, C, D, E and G. You are applying the same interval idea from a new tonic. FROM READING TO PLAYING Try it yourself. Play the same short phrase in E Aeolian and E Dorian.
